extracted.intended_audience: romance writers, editors, and readers interested in inclusive representation
extracted.subtask_description: A resource list and practical guidance for reading and writing romance that represents diverse identities respectfully and accurately, with pointers for language, characterization, editing, and small craft techniques that make stories welcoming to marginalized readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use romance to model personal growth and inclusion
rubrics_metrics.description: The best romance stories give us examples of people going through a process of self-discovery in the shifting landscape of close relationships.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Leverage the skills-building arc of romance—accepting responsibility for growth, dismantling judgments, healing wounds, and championing equality—to make stories that also serve as models for inclusion in society. Treat inclusion as part of character development rather than an add-on.

rubrics_metrics.name: Portray Black romance beyond struggle (joyful representation)
rubrics_metrics.description: "The black experience in America isn't all about struggle. ... black romance novels remind us it's also about joy." (from "Black Romance Novels Matter Too")
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid limiting Black characters to narratives of trauma or struggle; include joy, ordinary pleasures, and full emotional lives. Seek stories that reflect the diversity of Black experiences rather than tokenizing or confining them to hardship.

rubrics_metrics.name: Actively combat racism and increase diversity in romance publishing
rubrics_metrics.description: Discussion of the long debate about racism and diversity in romantic fiction (e.g., "Fifty Shades of White: The Long Fight Against Racism in Romance Novels").
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware of historical exclusion and take concrete steps to include diverse voices and stories. Recognize systemic issues in the genre and work toward equitable representation and opportunities for authors from marginalized communities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure LGBTQ readers can find themselves on the page
rubrics_metrics.description: "Losing yourself in a book requires finding at least a shred of yourself in the story." (from "Reader, He Married Him: LGBTQ Romance’s Search for Happily-Ever-After")
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include authentic queer characters, relationships, and experiences so queer readers can see themselves represented. Avoid erasure, invisibility, or tokenism; strive for scenes and details that affirm queer identity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use small, reality-affirming details (the "shoulder check") for queer inclusivity
rubrics_metrics.description: A shoulder check: "It's... an easy win... a dash of reality affirming what it's like to be a queer guy in a public space with another queer guy and considering a kiss."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include brief, believable moments that normalize queer presence (e.g., a glance, an unselfconscious public gesture) to make scenes feel realistic and welcoming without drawing excessive attention to difference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid casually racist tropes and behaviors
rubrics_metrics.description: Reference to "7 Casually Racist Things That White Authors Do" which catalogs everyday racist patterns white authors repeat.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Learn common microaggressions and narrative habits that perpetuate racism; unlearn them. Audit your prose for stereotyping, othering, exoticizing, or treating characters of color as props for white protagonists' growth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Represent introversion respectfully and accurately
rubrics_metrics.description: Materials like "Caring for Your Introvert" and the Introvert, Dear community emphasize that introverts are often misunderstood and have different needs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid pathologizing quietness or using introversion as shorthand for weakness. Portray introverted characters' interiority, needs, and strengths authentically and avoid clichés.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid ableist language; consult glossaries of ableist phrases
rubrics_metrics.description: "Ableism/Language / Glossary of Ableist Phrases" and "Violence in Language: Circling Back to Linguistic Ableism": language is embedded with sexism, heterosexism, cissexism, binarism, and racism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scrutinize word choices for ableist origins or uses. Use published glossaries and resources to identify problematic terms, replace them with respectful alternatives, and understand the cultural impact of language choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: When writing characters different from you, learn and ask rather than assume
rubrics_metrics.description: "Writing the Other" guidance: "People are different. There are things we don’t get about each other. Usually it’s because we haven’t asked."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Take classes, consult subject-matter and cultural experts, seek sensitivity readers, and do research. Aim to write characters 'sensitively and convincingly' by listening, asking questions, and centering lived experience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be mindful of fetishization and outsider dynamics in M/M and other queer fictions
rubrics_metrics.description: Referencing scholarship like "What To Do If Your Inner Tomboy Is a Homo: Straight Women, Bisexuality, and Pleasure in M/M Gay Romance Fictions" which addresses controversy around outsiders deriving erotic pleasure from marginalized stories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider ethical implications when writing about communities you are not part of (e.g., voyeurism, fetishization, commodification). Reflect on reader impacts and whether representations respect the humanity of characters rather than reducing them to erotic objects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Follow Progressive Style Guide commitments for non-discriminatory language
rubrics_metrics.description: "A Progressive's Style Guide" commits to: 1) We combat discriminatory language. 2) We seek advice or more information when we’re unsure. 3) When writing, speaking, or using images, we aim to use examples that reflect a broad range of identities and perspectives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt editorial policies that explicitly oppose discriminatory language, require consultation when unsure, and prioritize inclusive examples. Use these commitments during revision, copyediting, and publication to reduce harm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use copyediting as a tool for access, inclusion, and liberation
rubrics_metrics.description: "Radical copyediting helps language live up to its most radical potential—serving the ends of access, inclusion, and liberation, rather than maintaining oppression and the status quo."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Let editorial interventions advance equity: flag problematic phrasing, suggest inclusive alternatives, and prioritize clarity and accessibility for marginalized readers rather than preserving conventions that uphold exclusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Promote accessibility and diverse staffing in editorial/publishing services
rubrics_metrics.description: Tessera Editorial: founded on making publishing accessible and opening books to as many readers as possible through diverse voices in the profession; an editorial company of all BIPOC, all remote.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Support or hire diverse editors, consider remote/accessible workflows, and ensure editorial teams include people from the communities being represented to improve authenticity and equity in publishing.
